risks: No participants are involved; the risk is a review that overstates benefit and leads the unit to push diaries on families who find them distressing.
consent: Not applicable to the review itself; the guideline it informs will describe consent for diary writing, photographs and later reading.
data: Only published and publicly available material is used; the unit's uptake figure (118 of 231 families) is quoted in aggregate with the unit manager's agreement.
equity: PROGRESS-Plus: families with a different main language, without a regular visitor or able to visit only at night are offered diaries less often. The review reports delivery by these groups where studies allow and recommends translated guides and an offer at the first family meeting.
effectiveness: Success is a guideline that uses the review's certainty statements, not a claim that diaries prevent post-traumatic stress.
efficiency: Forty hours of existing staff time and a library search; no new cost.
costs: Staff time already approved; no purchases.
grants: None needed; a later local evaluation of the diary programme could apply to the hospital's nursing research fund.
partnerships: Hospital librarian, the unit's nurse educator as second checker, two former patients and one relative from the follow-up clinic's advisory group to read the draft.
rebPath: No research ethics review is needed for a review of published literature; if the unit later evaluates its own programme with patient data, that work goes to the research ethics board.
limitations: A narrative review, even structured, is more open to selective emphasis than a systematic review; one main reviewer; English-language bias.
summary: No participants; equity reporting by language and family presence; research ethics review only for any later local evaluation.
